Introduction and meaning
Abduction (old 362): compelling by force, or inducing by deceitful means, a person to go from any place. Abduction is not an offence by itself — it is the in-order-to sections (140, 87, etc.) that punish. BNS restatement of IPC 362. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 138 is the rule on “Abduction”. The section provides that whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 138 exists so that “Abduction” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
138. Whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person

hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 138 (Abduction), Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 138 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 138 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

Meaning. Abduction (old 362): compelling by force, or inducing by deceitful means, a person to go from any place. Abduction is not an offence by itself — it is the in-order-to sections (140, 87, etc.) that punish. BNS restatement of IPC 362. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.

Legal rule. In student language: BNS s. 138 is the rule on “Abduction”. The section provides that whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person. Do not stop at the heading. 1. Whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person

Illustration. Give one short original example (label it as an example) and apply the ingredients.

Comprehensive Written Submissions. Deepen the doctrinal synthesis with four foundational layers.

Layer 1 — Place the section in the Chapter. Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.. Show why this heading sits where it sits.

learningObjectives: Master the definition and legal characteristics of abduction under BNS s. 138.
Analyze the two alternative statutory means: force (compulsion) or deceit (inducement).
Understand that abduction is an auxiliary concept that is not punishable in isolation without an aggravated criminal intent.
Contrast abduction with kidnapping across age, means, and consent.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 138 defines abduction: whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Defines the non-autonomous movement of a person accomplished through physical force or fraudulent deceit, serving as the foundational predicate for aggravated personal liberty crimes.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 138 (corresponding to IPC s. 362).
Two alternative modalities: (1) Compulsion by force; (2) Inducement by deceitful means.
Target: Any person of any age or gender.
Movement: Causing the person to go from any place.
Auxiliary nature: Section 138 defines abduction; substantive punishment attaches only when combined with intent to murder, ransom, confine, or force marriage (ss. 87, 140, etc.).
essentialIngredients: A person was compelled or induced to go from any place.
The movement was accomplished by force (physical compulsion); OR
The movement was accomplished by deceitful means (fraudulent misrepresentation).
The victim did not move voluntarily with true consent.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 138 carries forward IPC 362, defining 'abduction'. A vital doctrine of criminal law is that abduction is NOT a standalone substantive offence. Merely compelling or tricking someone into moving from one place to another is not punishable by itself under Section 138; it becomes a punishable crime only when coupled with a specific felonious intent defined in other sections (such as abduction to compel marriage under s. 87, abduction to murder or extort ransom under s. 140, or abduction for wrongful confinement under s. 142). Unlike kidnapping, which applies only to minors or persons of unsound mind, abduction applies to any living human being of any age. Furthermore, while kidnapping requires no force or fraud, abduction strictly requires either actual physical force (compelling movement) or deceitful means (misrepresenting facts to trick the victim into moving).
examples: Teaching example (Compulsion by force): Assailants force an adult business executive into a car at gunpoint and drive him to another district. This is abduction by force under s. 138 (punishable under s. 140 for ransom).

Teaching example (Deceitful inducement): An accused falsely tells a woman that her mother has suffered a cardiac arrest and is dying at a clinic twenty miles away, offering to drive her there, but actually drives her to a secluded warehouse to confine her. This is abduction by deceitful means.
distinctions: Abduction (s. 138) vs Kidnapping (s. 137): Kidnapping is restricted to minors/unsound mind, requires no force/fraud, and is a substantive offence; Abduction applies to any age, requires force or fraud, and is an auxiliary concept.
Abduction by Force vs Abduction by Deceit: Force involves physical coercion or immediate threats; Deceit involves fraudulent falsehoods misleading the will of the victim.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who told a job seeker that an interview was scheduled at an out-of-town estate, inducing the job seeker to travel there where he was locked up, abducted the victim.
Rule: Inducing any person by deceitful means to go from any place constitutes abduction under BNS s. 138.
Application: The interview was completely fictitious, serving as deceitful means inducing physical movement.
Conclusion: The act constitutes abduction under BNS s. 138 (chargeable substantively with wrongful confinement).

keyTakeaways: Defines abduction as compelling by force or inducing by deceit to go from any place.
Applies to persons of any age, gender, or mental capacity.
Requires actual force or fraudulent deceit.
Auxiliary definition; substantive punishment requires companion sections (e.g. s. 140).
